an3.117:2.2: While the presence of these defilements needs no explanation as a “failure in mind”, the text’s intent is quite specific. These are manifestations of greed and hate, which are primarily overcome through development of samādhi. Compare the “covetousness and displeasure” that are curbed through sense restraint ([an3.16:2.3]()) and eliminated in mindfulness meditation ([an3.156:5.2]()). Here, then, as so often, “mind” implies the development of the mind in samādhi.
an3.117:3.3: This nihilist doctrine (_natthikavāda_) is attributed to Ajita of the Hair Blanket at [dn2:23.2](). | While this view denies the efficacy or moral actions, it goes further to state that there is no such thing as that which is “given”. To be “given” is to assume a giver and receiver, and the relationship between them. In Ajita’s belief, there is only matter devoid of meaning, so what others see as “given” to him is no different than anything else. | The denial of “mother and father” is usually interpreted as the denial of moral duty toward one’s parents. However, I think it is a doctrine of conception which denies that a child is created by the mother and father. Rather, the child is produced by the four elements, with parents as mere instigators and incubators. | Compare Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23 on the liberated Self, “A father is not a father, a mother is not a mother, worlds are not worlds, gods are not gods, and Vedas are not Vedas. Here a thief is not a thief, an abortionist is not an abortionist, an outcaste is not an outcaste, a pariah is not a pariah, a recluse is not a recluse, and an ascetic is not an ascetic. Neither the good nor the bad follows him, for he has now passed beyond all sorrows of the heart.”
an3.117:6.3: Elsewhere defined in terms of the four absorptions ([dn8:19.11]()).
